summary:
Consensual sex between men is a criminal offence in Kiribati, carrying five to fourteen years' imprisonment depending on the offence charged. A 2015 US State Department human rights report recorded no prosecutions under the provision. The same report listed Kiribati, alongside Sri Lanka, among the states still maintaining anti-homosexuality laws in 2016, in the context of the UN General Assembly's 84–77 rejection of an amendment that would have defunded the Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity.

The Constitution of Kiribati bars discrimination by race, national origin and colour. It does not extend that guarantee to sexual orientation or gender identity, and no such non-discrimination statute was in force at the time of reporting. Gender-based discrimination is prohibited only in the field of employment, and the State Department observed that this narrow protection is poorly enforced.

Land ownership is restricted to I-Kiribati, a constitutional limitation affecting property rights rather than entry, but relevant to any longer stay.

At the 21st session of the Universal Periodic Review, France, Slovenia and Chile urged Kiribati to decriminalise homosexuality. The Kiribati delegation made no response to those recommendations, while stating that it was considering Uruguay's advice to adopt legislation prohibiting discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual identity and sexual orientation. Whether that legislation was enacted is not established by the sources.

No cases of societal discrimination or violence against LGBT people were reported to the State Department in 2015. That is an absence of documented cases, not a finding of safety, and the sources carry no trans-specific violence data.

The sources address no rules on legal gender recognition, gender markers on passports or identity documents, bathroom or facility access, entry screening, or access to gender-affirming care. A visitor should treat those areas as unassessed rather than permissive.
tangentialFactors:
Ethnographic literature documents a locally grounded gender-diverse role, the Pinapinaaine or Binabinaaine, shared with Tuvalu and discussed in Besnier's 2014 study “Gender on the edge”. The University of Hawai'i at Manoa research guide on gender identity and sexual identity in the Pacific notes that such Pacific identity expressions are rendered as homosexual or transgender only through Western vocabulary, so imported categories of trans identity may not map onto local ones.

Kiribati's position in 2016 was set against sustained external pressure: three states pressed for decriminalisation at the Universal Periodic Review, and the state was singled out in a UN General Assembly report for retaining anti-homosexuality laws. Delegation silence on the decriminalisation recommendations, paired with openness on a non-discrimination statute, indicates the direction of official engagement without indicating change in the criminal law.

The 2015 observation that no societal discrimination or violence was reported contrasts with the criminal statute itself, which remains a standing legal exposure for men who have sex with men and for anyone perceived to fall within it.
localsOnly:
I-Kiribati hold constitutional protection against discrimination by race, national origin and colour, and restricted land ownership rights that are not available to non-citizens.

Residents' protection against gender discrimination is confined to employment and was assessed as poorly enforced. Sexual orientation and gender identity are not covered by any non-discrimination law, and the government indicated in 2015 only that it was considering such legislation.

Criminal liability for consensual sex between men applies domestically at five to fourteen years' imprisonment; no prosecutions were reported as of 2015.

The Pinapinaaine/Binabinaaine role is documented in Kiribati as well as Tuvalu in Pacific anthropological work, indicating an established local gender expression distinct from Western trans and homosexual categories.
outOfScopeNotes:
The most recent status evidence in the inventory dates from 2015 and 2016. Whether the criminal provision still stands, whether prosecutions have occurred since, and whether the contemplated non-discrimination legislation covering gender, sexual identity and sexual orientation was enacted are unresolved on these sources.

No source addresses legal gender recognition, amendment of gender markers on passports or national identity documents, or the interaction of those documents with immigration control; this is not stated as absent law, only as unsourced.

Hate-crime provisions, police conduct toward gender-diverse people, facility and restroom access, healthcare access including gender-affirming care, and refugee or asylum pathways are not covered by the inventory.

The finding of no reported societal discrimination or violence derives from a single 2015 embassy-style reporting cycle and should be read as unverified rather than as a negative finding.

The relationship between local Kiribati gender roles and the legal category of sex in the criminal provision is not analysed in the sources.
